title: Learning Models of Individual Behavior in Chess

problem.claim: Human-oriented AI systems require predicting human actions rather than only optimal actions.

gap.claim: Existing work has mainly captured human behavior in aggregate, potentially limiting benefits for particular individuals.

contributions.claim: Develop highly accurate predictive models of individual human behavior in chess.
Improve prediction accuracy for a particular player's moves by applying fine-tuning methods to Maia, an open-source AlphaZero variant trained on human players.
Use personalized models for stylometry by predicting who made a given set of moves.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report significantly improved prediction accuracy for a particular player's moves after applying fine-tuning methods.
The authors report that personalized models can perform stylometry, indicating capture of human decision-making at an individual level.

narrative_sequence.summary: Human-like behavior capture is useful for learning, collaboration, and extended interaction with AI systems.
Human-oriented AI motivates predicting human actions rather than optimal actions, while prior work has focused on aggregate behavior.
The work develops individual-behavior prediction models in chess and fine-tunes Maia for particular players.
Personalized models are used for stylometry, predicting the player responsible for a set of moves.
The authors position individual behavior alignment as a path toward improved human-AI interaction.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the dataset size, player coverage, evaluation protocol, baseline results, or numerical accuracy.
The abstract does not describe the fine-tuning methods in detail.
The abstract does not establish independent verification, generalization beyond chess, or deployment outcomes.
